title: Axiomatic Atlas: A Prescriptive Framework for Neural Architecture Design
claim: Audit an architecture against composable axiom classes to get certificates that locate failures in design space and imply targeted repairs.
layout: Left-to-right flow across 4 regions; 3D surfaces and design-space blobs with repair inset
description: A wide left-to-right diagram. At far left, a standard-attention mini flowchart (query Q and key K into Dot Product, softmax, attention score) sits above a blob labeled Neural Architecture Families, which holds a grid and colored dashed regions with red and black dots. A thick arrow leads to a 2x2 grid of small square grids labeled Structural (S), Primitive (P), Stability (E) and Merge (M), titled Axiomatic Atlas. Above them, bracketed 3D surfaces in orange, green and blue show Certificate Factors. Curved arrows lead to the large right panel, a gray 3D surface over overlapping red, blue, green and orange ellipses called Neural Architecture Design Space. A dashed vertical line with black points marks collapse, and a red arrow marks the repair. The panel's legend separates solid healthy bound from dashed collapse regime. At far right, an OrthoKV flowchart replaces direct Q and K with Project boxes.
caption: Overview of the Axiomatic Atlas framework. Nodes denote feature tensors and directed edges denote operator applications. A neural architecture (left: standard attention) is audited against four axiom classes (S, P, E, M), producing certificate factors that locate the design in axiom space. Collapse is encoded by factors approaching the dashed zero-boundary; repair is encoded as a targeted graph/operator modification (right: OrthoKV) that restores the solid healthy-bound region.
abstract: Neural architecture design lacks first principles: innovations are discovered empirically and justified post-hoc, with no systematic way to diagnose *why* an architecture fails or derive *what* repair will succeed. We introduce the *Axiomatic Atlas*, encoding requirements as composable axioms over graph connectivity, operator contracts, numerical stability, and information preservation. Given an operator library and wiring conventions, the Atlas constructs certificates lower-bounding output variation via min-cut analysis and diagnoses failures by locating axiom violations. Crucially, the framework is prescriptive: each violation implies a targeted repair, reducing architecture design to constraint satisfaction. We prove variation bounds under exact and finite-precision arithmetic, enabling modular verification across transformers, MoEs, SSMs, and GNNs. Four Atlas-derived interventions validate the approach: +46 percentage points on GNN bottlenecks, $3\times$ robustness to MoE quantization, 83\% gap closure with adaptive expert budgets, and 0\%$\to$100\% retrieval via orthogonal keys---each against matched negative controls.
